text: Every point in tennis starts off with a serve. It is a vast vast majority of the time hit overhead. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: the dominant hand should be holding a grip on the bottom of the racket grip called the continental or hammer grip while the non-dominant hand holds the ball. Stance: with both feet baseline, the server needs to stand to either side of the centre mark line. Start with both chest and feet pointing to the dominant-side net post. Your dominant foot should be staggered behind the other foot with its toe in line behind the non-dominant heel. The racket swing until trophy position: start with both hands relaxed and down your body. Raise both arms up. The trophy position: the trophy position is the body position of the player typically erected into a trophy. With the non-dominant arm pointing all the way up, the dominant elbow just below shoulder level, racket pointing upwards to the sky and knees bent into a quarter-squat position. Trophy position swing into contact: As the racket drops down the player’s spine and swings up towards the ball, the non-dominant arm should be pulled down and legs should drive the body up and off the ground. Contact: should be made with the entire body extended upwards, chest stays up, and dominant arm fully extended with the racket. Different ways of contact cause a different spin to occur to the ball. The player should feel a sense of pronation when serving. Follow through: after contact, the racket should finish down by the lower half of the non-dominant side of the body. Player should be only landing on the non-dominant foot, just inside the baseline. COMMON MISTAKES: Hitting the ball in the net: caused by the body not driving upwards during the serve. Fix: The player should aim to keep their chest up tall at contact and chin up on the landing. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: caused by hitting under the ball during the serve. Hitting the ball out in terms of width: caused by the player throwing their body around at contact and/or hitting the ball at an extreme angle. Fix: keeping the chest facing the ball at contact and the racket face should face where the player is aiming at contact. Mishitting the ball: when the ball hits the player’s racket frame instead of the strings. Fix: Keep the head and chest still at contact and facing the ball.

The backhand is a shot hit on the player’s non-dominant side of their body. For a left-handed player, the shot is hit on the right side and vice versa. It is typically hit with two hands, but one hand is also used too. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: the dominant hand should be on the bottom of the racket grip, with the non-dominant hand right above it. The dominant hand should be holding the racket like a hammer called the continental or hammer grip and the non-dominant hand should be holding the grip like a handshake. Preparation: Requires a unit turn of the upper body where the dominant shoulder is under the player's chin, chest face to the non-dominant side of the court. BALANCE AND MOVEMENT — FOUNDATION PHILOSOPHY Everything starts with balanced movement. Without balance, everything else the student performs is redundant. A balanced player can correctly position themselves relative to the ball and perform complex actions to manipulate it. Balance is taught before any technique — a student must be able to move with balance before they swing at the ball. PROGRESSION — complete each before moving on: 1. Student moves to the ball with balance, no swing. 2. Student balances on both feet whilst hitting. 3. Student balances on either foot whilst hitting. WHAT BALANCED MOVEMENT LOOKS LIKE: - Chest upright before, during, and after the shot. - Head still — eyes track the ball all the way to racket contact, not lifting early to see where the ball goes. - Weight on balls of feet, knees slightly bent in ready position. - After the shot, player can hold their

contact, not lifting early to see where the ball goes. - Weight on balls of feet, knees slightly bent in ready position. - After the shot, player can hold their finish position without stumbling. COMMON BALANCE ERRORS IN TENNIS: - Moving feet, torso or head during the swing: caused by late positioning — the student is still arriving at the ball when they swing, so the body is still in motion. Fix: get there early, stop, then swing. - Torso collapsing after the shot: caused by rushing to recover before finishing the swing, or weak. core engagement through contact. Fix: think about finishing the shot before recovering back. CUES FOR BALANCE: - "Hold your finish until the your shot bounces" - "Pretend you're standing on a surfboard — stay centred" - "Move your feet, then swing — not at the same time" DRILLS FOR BALANCE: Drill 1 — Stop and

- "Pretend you're standing on a surfboard — stay centred" - "Move your feet, then swing — not at the same time" DRILLS FOR BALANCE: Drill 1 — Stop and Swing: Coach feeds balls to various positions. Student must move to the ball, stop both feet completely, swing, and freeze the finish position until the ball lands on the other side. If the student moves during the swing the rep doesn't count. Start slow, increase feed pace as balance improves.

The forehand needs to involve making the ball spin forwards, also known as topspin. Without topspin, it is more difficult to hit the ball measurably without losing control. The forehand is hit on the player’s dominant side of the body, for example a right handed player’s forehand is hit on the right side of the player’s body. It can be hit with two hands, but it is suggested to use one for the vast majority of the time. There are 3 main ways of holding the racket grip for a forehand: eastern, semi-western, and western grip. Most players use the semi-western grip for the best of both worlds. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: Semi-western for most players. Hold the grip palm down, pretending to flip on egg on a pan. Preparation: Non-dominant shoulder under player’s chin, non-dominant arm extended out to the side, chest face the side, racket points up to the sky, and dominant arm’s elbow away from the body with space in the armpit. The racket swing until contact point: let the racket drop down and push the dominant side’s hip towards the ball. The hip push should lead the racket arm towards the ball to make contact. As the racket swings towards the non-dominant arm should pull itself towards the body and finish on the players chest. Contact point: the contact point should have the racket face facing either straight to the ball or slightly closed downwards. It should not face upwards to the sky at all. Ideally the contact point should be in front of the body, with the dominant arm’s elbow away from the body. Follow through:

Follow through: After contact, the racket arm should be extended out towards where the player is aiming and eventually wrap around the non-dominant side of the body. The follow through should have the racket face that made contact with the ball, facing the non-dominant side of the player. For example, the racket face should finish facing to the left side of a right handed player. The dominant elbow should finish towards the centre line of the body and away from it. The height of where the follow through finishes depends on how much spin and arc is wanted of the shot. Lower finish means less arc and spin, higher finish means more arc and spin.
